title: Rolling, sliding, spinning, swinging and bouncing: five ways things move

summary.text: Give a round steel dabba the same push twice. On its side, it rolls far. Standing flat, it slides a little and stops. Things move in five main ways: they roll, slide, spin, swing and bounce. Your child moves in all five ways, hunts for them at home, and finds that rolling goes much further than sliding.
summary.art: A girl kneeling on a tiled floor watching a round steel dabba roll far away on its side, while a second dabba standing flat has stopped close to her.

intro.hook: Can you move your body in five different ways? Try to roll, slide, spin, swing and bounce.
intro.text: Things move in different ways. A ball rolls. A chappal slides on a wet floor. A fan spins. A swing swings. A ball bounces. In this unit you move in all five ways, find them at home, and push one dabba two ways: does it go further when it rolls or when it slides?
intro.art: A small girl on a mat in a flat, rolling sideways, while a ceiling fan spins above her and a cloth bag swings on the door handle.

outcomes: By the end I can say the five ways things move: roll, slide, spin, swing and bounce.
By the end I can show each of the five ways with my own body.
By the end I can find things at home that roll, slide, spin, swing or bounce.
By the end I can say that rolling goes further than sliding with the same push, and why.
By the end I can say that a thing bounces when it squashes and springs back.
By the end I can make a guess, test it, and say what I saw.

terms.meaning: Motion means moving. Anything that is moving is in motion.
terms.example: A running dog, a falling leaf and a turning fan are all in motion.
terms.art: A dog running, a leaf falling and a ceiling fan turning, on one page.

terms.meaning: To roll is to turn over and over while moving along. Only part of a rolling thing touches the floor at a time.
terms.example: A ball rolls across the floor. A lemon rolls off the table.
terms.art: A ball rolling across a tiled floor, with little curved arrows showing it turning over.

terms.meaning: To slide is to move along while the same part keeps touching the floor and rubbing on it.
terms.example: A plate slides when you push it across the table. Your socks slide on a smooth floor.
terms.art: A steel plate sliding across a table, with a straight arrow and a little rub line under it.

terms.meaning: To spin is to turn round and round in one place. A spinning thing turns round its middle.
terms.example: A ceiling fan spins. A top spins on its point.
terms.art: A wooden top spinning on a floor, with a curved arrow round it.

terms.meaning: To swing is to move back and forth, hanging from one point.
terms.example: A swing on a rope goes back and forth. Your arms swing when you walk.
terms.art: A girl on a rope swing hanging from a tree branch, with a curved arrow going both ways.

terms.meaning: To bounce is to hit something and spring back off it. A bouncing thing squashes a little, then springs back to its shape.
terms.example: A rubber ball bounces up from the floor. A ball of atta dough does not.
terms.art: A rubber ball bouncing up from a floor, drawn a little squashed where it touches.

explanations.definition: Most moving things roll, slide, spin, swing or bounce. Many things can move in more than one of these ways.
explanations.description: A ball can roll, spin and bounce. A steel plate can slide, spin and roll. How a thing moves depends on how it is pushed and how it touches the floor.
examples: A ball rolls on the floor, spins on a finger and bounces off a wall.
Your body can roll on a mat, slide in socks, spin round, swing your arms and bounce on the spot.
A steel plate slides on the table, spins when you twist it and rolls when you stand it on its edge.
explanations.context: This card is about the five ways of moving you tried in Five Ways With My Body: roll, slide, spin, swing and bounce.
explanations.art: Five small drawings in a row: a rolling ball, a sliding plate, a spinning top, a swinging bag and a bouncing ball.

explanations.definition: With the same push, a thing that rolls goes much further than the same thing sliding, because rolling rubs the floor far less.
explanations.description: In the Roll or Slide Test, when the dabba slid standing flat, its whole flat bottom rubbed along the floor, and the rubbing stopped it soon. When the dabba rolled on its side, each part touched the floor for a moment and lifted off again, so it hardly rubbed. The rubbing that slows things down is called friction. This is why wheels make heavy things easier to move.
examples: In the Roll or Slide Test, the dabba on its side rolled many tiles. Standing flat, it slid only one or two.
A suitcase with wheels is easy to pull. Without wheels, it scrapes and is hard to drag.
Gas cylinders are tipped onto their round edge and rolled, not dragged.
explanations.context: This card is about the Roll or Slide Test, where you pushed the same dabba lying on its side and standing flat.
explanations.art: One dabba rolling on its side with a long arrow, and the same dabba standing flat with a short arrow and rub lines under it.

explanations.concept: Bouncing is squashing and springing back
explanations.definition: A thing bounces when it squashes as it hits the floor and then springs back to its shape, pushing itself up.
explanations.description: A rubber ball squashes a tiny bit when it hits the floor. Then it springs back to round, and that pushes it up off the floor. Dough squashes and stays squashed, so it does not bounce.
examples: In the Bounce Test, the rubber ball bounced high and the dough ball went splat.
A crumpled paper ball bounced a little, because the paper springs back only a little.
Your knees bend and straighten when you bounce on the spot.
explanations.context: This card is about the Bounce Test, where you dropped different balls from the same height.
explanations.art: A rubber ball bouncing high next to a flat, squashed ball of dough on the floor.

explanations.concept: Spinning and swinging go round a still point
explanations.definition: A spinning thing turns round its middle, which stays in one place. A swinging thing hangs from one point and moves back and forth below it.
explanations.description: When a fan spins, the middle of the fan stays put while the blades go round it. When a bag swings on a door handle, the handle stays still while the bag goes back and forth under it. A swing slows down and stops in the end, unless someone pushes it again.
examples: A ceiling fan spins round its middle.
A bag on a door handle swings back and forth under the handle.
The whole Earth spins round once every day, carrying us with it.
explanations.context: This card is about the Spin It and Swing It activities, where you spun a plate and swung a bag.
explanations.art: A ceiling fan with a dot at its still middle, next to a cloth bag swinging on a door handle with a dot at the handle.

agreed.text: With the same push, rolling things go further than sliding things.
agreed.evidence: A dabba on its side rolls across a room. The same dabba standing flat slides a short way and stops. Wheels make carts, cycles and suitcases easy to move.

agreed.text: Things bounce because they squash and spring back.
agreed.evidence: Slow-motion films show a ball squashing flat where it hits the floor, then springing back as it leaves. Dough, which does not spring back, does not bounce.

agreed.text: The Earth spins round once a day.
agreed.evidence: The Sun, the Moon and the stars all seem to move across the sky once a day. Photos from space show the Earth turning.

challenging.who: A common first guess among young children
challenging.for: Balls, lemons and bottles on their side all roll away.
challenging.against: In the Roll or Slide Test, the round dabba standing flat did not roll. It slid. A round thing rolls only when its round side touches the floor.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that round things always roll.

challenging.claim: Each thing has only one way of moving.
challenging.who: A common idea, because we often say 'a ball rolls' or 'a fan spins'
challenging.for: We usually see a ball rolling and a fan spinning.
challenging.against: A ball can roll, spin, swing in a string bag and bounce. A steel plate can slide, spin and roll. How a thing moves depends on how it is pushed and how it touches the floor.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that each thing moves in only one way.

challenging.against: An empty plastic bottle, a crumpled paper ball and your own body on a mattress all bounce. Anything that squashes and springs back can bounce.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that only balls can bounce.

big_questions.q: In the Roll or Slide Test, the dabba was the same both times. Why did it go so much further when it rolled?
big_questions.hint: Think about which part of the dabba touched the floor each time.

big_questions.q: Why does a ball of dough not bounce, when a rubber ball does?
big_questions.hint: Look at the dough after it lands. Did it go back to round?

big_questions.q: The Earth is spinning right now. Why can't you feel it?
big_questions.hint: Do you feel a smooth train moving when your eyes are shut?

big_questions.q: When you sit very still, is any part of you still moving?
big_questions.hint: Put a hand on your chest. Feel your breath.

story.title: Kanmani and the Rice Tin
text: Kanmani was six. She lived on the third floor of a block of flats in Chennai, with her Amma and her Paati. Paati is her grandmother.
One morning the doorbell rang. It was Selvi akka, who brings the gas cylinders. A new red cylinder stood by the lift.
"That looks so heavy," said Kanmani. "How will you get it to the kitchen?"

Selvi akka smiled. She tipped the cylinder a little, so it stood on the round edge of its bottom. Then she turned it with both hands. The cylinder rolled on its edge, round and round, across the floor and into the kitchen.
"Dragging is hard work," said Selvi akka. "When I drag it, the whole bottom rubs on the floor. When I roll it, it just turns, and only a little bit touches the floor at a time."
After Selvi akka left, Kanmani wanted to try. Paati said, "Only grown-ups move gas cylinders. But you can try with something else."

Kanmani found the big steel rice tin. It was round, like a drum, and half full of rice. She stood behind it and pushed. The tin scraped and squeaked on the floor. It moved a tiny bit, then stopped. Her arms ached.
Paati checked that the lid was shut tight. Then she laid the tin down on its side. "Now push," she said.
Kanmani gave it a small push. The tin rolled! It rolled all the way across the kitchen and bumped gently into the door.
Kanmani stared. "It's the same tin. It has the same rice. I'm the same me. But now it goes!"
"It's the same tin," said Paati, "but it is touching the floor in a different way. Standing up, its flat bottom rubbed the floor. Lying down, it rolled."

All afternoon, Kanmani looked for ways that things move. An onion fell off the counter and rolled under the fridge. Her socks slid on the smooth floor. The ceiling fan spun round and round. Amma's cloth bag swung on the door handle. Her rubber ball bounced off the wall.
"Everything has its own way of moving," said Kanmani. "Balls roll and fans spin."
"Watch," said Paati. She put a steel plate flat on the floor and pushed it. It slid. She twisted it, and it spun. She stood it on its edge and gave it a push, and it rolled away in a wobbly line.
Kanmani laughed. "The same plate did three things!"
"It did," said Paati. "How a thing moves depends on how you push it and how it touches the floor."

That night, Kanmani lay in bed and rolled over. "I can roll," she thought. "I can slide on the floor in my socks. I can spin, and swing my arms, and bounce on my toes." She rolled over once more, and fell asleep.
story.note: Chennai is a real city in Tamil Nadu. Paati means grandmother in Tamil, and akka means elder sister, used for a young woman. Gas delivery workers in India often tip a cylinder onto its bottom edge and roll it. Children should never move gas cylinders. Kanmani, Paati, Amma and Selvi are made up.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Kanmani thinks the heavy tin will not move. It slides only a little standing up, but rolls easily on its side. The tin did not change, only how it touched the floor. Then the plate shows that one thing can slide, spin or roll. How a thing moves depends on how it is pushed and how it meets the floor.
ask: How did Selvi akka move the heavy cylinder?
Why did the rice tin go further when it was lying down?
What three things did Paati's plate do?
Which of the five ways can you move?
art: A young woman in a sari tipping a red gas cylinder onto its bottom edge and rolling it into a flat's kitchen, while a girl watches from the doorway.
A girl pushing a tall steel rice tin standing on a kitchen floor, her face scrunched up, the tin hardly moving.
The same rice tin lying on its side, rolling across the kitchen towards the door, the girl's arms out and her mouth open.
A grandmother in a cotton sari spinning a steel plate on the floor while the girl laughs.

experiments.title: The Roll or Slide Test: does a dabba go further rolling or sliding?
experiments.context: This is the main experiment of the unit. You give the same round dabba the same push twice: once lying on its side, and once standing flat. Which way does it go further?
experiments.question: With the same push, does a round dabba go further when it rolls on its side or when it slides standing flat?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the dabba go further lying on its side or standing flat? Or the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same dabba, the same book and the same push every time. The book always moves from the start line to the stop line, then stops. Only the way the dabba sits changes. We try each way 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a round steel dabba or tiffin box with its lid on, short and wide, about the size of your hand, or a roll of cello tape
a hardback book or a flat chopping board, to push with
a smooth floor as long as you can find, at least 6 big steps, such as a tiled room or a corridor
2 strips of tape or 2 chalk lines, one hand-width apart, for the start and stop lines
6 small paper slips or bottle caps to mark where the dabba stops

schedule.what: Guess, push the dabba 3 times on its side and 3 times standing flat, mark where it stops, and count the tiles.

experiments.record: Draw the dabba on its side and standing flat. Next to each, draw a line that shows how far it went.

setup.art: A tiled floor with two tape lines one hand-width apart. A hardback book stands with its front edge on the first line, and a round steel dabba lies on its side touching the front of the book.
setup.caption: 1. Put the dabba touching the front of the book, at the start line.

setup.art: A girl's hands sliding a book from the start line to the stop line and stopping it there, and the dabba rolling away across the tiles.
setup.caption: 2. Slide the book to the stop line and stop. Watch the dabba go.

setup.art: The same dabba standing flat on its bottom, touching the book at the start line, and two paper slips on the floor marking where it stopped before.
setup.caption: 3. Now stand the dabba flat. Give it the same push.

flow.do: 1. Stick two tape lines on the floor, one hand-width apart. 2. Show your child the dabba and the book.
flow.say: This book is our pusher. The dabba sits touching the front of the book. You slide the book to the second line and stop. That is one push.
flow.kid: This book is your pusher. Slide it from one line to the next. Then stop.
flow.parent: Stopping the book at the second line keeps every push about the same. A short, wide dabba stands flat without tipping over. Close it tight. A roll of cello tape works just as well.

flow.do: 1. Hold the dabba on its side, then standing flat. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Write or draw the guess.
flow.say: First we lay the dabba on its side. Then we stand it flat. Which way will it go further? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which way will the dabba go further? On its side or standing flat? Why?

good: On its side it can roll.
Standing up it is flat, so it will stop.
It is the same dabba, so the same.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Write it down as your child says it. Do not explain yet.

flow.do: 1. Lay the dabba on its side, touching the book. 2. Your child pushes 3 times. 3. Put a slip where it stops each time.
flow.say: Lay the dabba on its side, touching the book. Slide the book to the line and stop. Watch where the dabba stops. Put a slip there.
flow.kid: Lay the dabba on its side. Push with the book. Mark where it stops.
flow.parent: The round side must be on the floor, with the flat ends facing left and right. If the dabba curves into a wall, just try again. A rolling dabba often goes many tiles. If it reaches the end of the room, write "all the way". Push the same way each time, firmly enough that the standing dabba slides.

flow.do: 1. Stand the dabba flat at the same place, touching the book. 2. Your child pushes the same way 3 times. 3. Mark where it stops each time.
flow.say: Now stand the dabba flat. Push it the very same way. Where does it stop this time?
flow.kid: Stand the dabba up flat. Push it the same way. Mark where it stops.

good: It slid a tiny bit and stopped.
It scraped on the floor.
It went much less far.

flow.parent: Standing flat, the dabba usually slides only a short way, often less than two tiles. Let your child hear the scrape.

flow.do: 1. Count the tiles to each slip together, or count hand-widths if your floor has no tiles. 2. Fill in the table. 3. Ask what your child saw and why.
flow.say: Let us count the tiles. Which way went further? What did you see? Why do you think it went further that way?
flow.kid: Count the tiles. Which way went further? Why, do you think?

ask.q: Why did it go further on its side?
good: It rolled.
Standing up, it rubbed on the floor.
Rolling only touches a little bit of the floor.

check.q: The same dabba got the same push. Which way did it go further?
check.why: Rolling hardly rubs the floor, so the dabba kept going. Sliding rubbed its whole flat bottom on the floor, so it stopped soon.

flow.parent: Now you can explain. Sliding rubs the whole bottom along the floor, and the rubbing stops the dabba. When the dabba rolls, each bit of it touches the floor and lifts off again, so it hardly rubs. Scientists call the rubbing friction.
flow.think: What else in our home has wheels to make it roll?

experiments.title: The Bounce Test: which balls bounce back up?
experiments.context: In this experiment you drop five kinds of ball from the same height. You watch which ones bounce back up and which do not.
experiments.question: Which of these bounce back up: a rubber ball, a ball of socks, a paper ball, a ball of atta dough, and an empty plastic bottle?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which ones will bounce high, which a little, and which not at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We drop every ball from the same height, the top of a table, onto the same floor. We let go without throwing. We drop each one 2 times.
results_table: What it did: high, a little, or no bounce

materials.item: a rubber ball or a tennis ball
a pair of socks rolled into a ball
a sheet of newspaper crumpled into a tight ball
a ball of atta dough or play clay, about the size of a lemon
an empty plastic bottle with its cap on
a table and a hard floor

schedule.what: Guess, drop each of the five balls twice from table height, and sort them into high, a little and no bounce.

experiments.record: Draw each thing and a curved line showing how high it bounced. Draw no line for things that did not bounce.

setup.art: Five things in a row on a table: a rubber ball, a ball of rolled socks, a crumpled newspaper ball, a ball of atta dough and an empty plastic bottle.
setup.caption: 1. Line up the five things on the table.

setup.art: A girl holding a rubber ball at the edge of a table and letting go, and the ball bouncing up from the tiled floor.
setup.caption: 2. Hold each one at the table edge. Let go.

setup.art: A ball of atta dough lying squashed flat on the floor, next to a rubber ball bouncing high.
setup.caption: 3. Look at each one after it lands.

flow.do: 1. Line up the five things. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason for each. 3. Write or draw the guesses.
flow.say: Here are five things to drop. Which will bounce high, which a little, and which not at all? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the five things. Which will bounce? Which will not? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the dough ball when it lands? Why?
good: It will go flat, because it is soft.
It will stick, because it is sticky.
It will squash, because it is squishy.

flow.parent: Write each guess down as your child says it. Do not explain yet.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds each thing at the edge of the table and lets go. 2. Drop each one twice. 3. Say together: high, a little, or no bounce.
flow.say: Hold it at the edge of the table. Let go, do not throw. Did it bounce high, a little, or not at all?
flow.kid: Hold it at the table edge. Let go. Did it bounce?
flow.parent: The rubber ball bounces high. The paper ball and the bottle bounce a little. The sock ball and the dough hardly bounce. Results can differ a little, and that is fine.

flow.do: 1. Pick up the dough ball and the rubber ball. 2. Look at their shapes. 3. Ask what is different.
flow.say: Look at the dough ball now. Look at the rubber ball. What is different about them after they landed?
flow.kid: Look at the dough. Look at the rubber ball. What changed?

good: It went flat.
It stayed squashed.
It did not go back to round.

flow.parent: Now explain. Both squash when they hit the floor. The rubber ball springs straight back to round, and that pushes it up. The dough stays squashed, so it does not bounce.

flow.do: 1. Squeeze the rubber ball, then the dough, in your child's hand. 2. Let go and watch.
flow.say: Squeeze the rubber ball, then let go. Now squeeze the dough. Which one springs back?
flow.kid: Squeeze the ball. Let go. Now squeeze the dough. Which springs back?

check.q: Why did the rubber ball bounce and the dough did not?
options: The ball springs back to its shape, and the dough stays squashed
The ball was dropped from higher
check.why: Both were dropped from the same height. The rubber ball springs back to round and pushes off the floor. The dough stays flat.

flow.think: What else at home springs back when you squeeze it?

activities.title: Five Ways With My Body: roll, slide, spin, swing, bounce
activities.context: In this activity you move your own body in the five ways: roll, slide, spin, swing and bounce. You feel how each one is different.

materials.item: a mat, a dari or a bed with a sheet
a pair of socks
a clear space on a smooth floor

activities.safety: Move furniture with corners out of the way. Slide slowly in socks, holding a grown-up's hand.

schedule.what: Roll on a mat, slide in socks, spin, swing your arms and bounce on the spot.

activities.record: Draw yourself doing your favourite one of the five.

setup.art: A girl lying on a dari, rolling sideways like a log, her arms above her head.
setup.caption: 1. Roll on a mat like a log.

setup.art: A girl in socks sliding slowly on a smooth tiled floor, holding a grown-up's hand.
setup.caption: 2. Slide in your socks, holding a hand.

setup.art: A girl spinning round with her arms out, then a boy swinging his arms, then a girl bouncing on her toes.
setup.caption: 3. Spin, swing your arms, and bounce.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the mat. 2. Show your child how to lie down and roll sideways like a log.
flow.say: Lie down on the mat. Now roll over and over, like a log. That is rolling.
flow.kid: Lie on the mat. Roll over and over. That is rolling!

ask.q: Which part of you touched the mat as you rolled?
good: My back, then my side, then my tummy.
A different part each time.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts on socks. 2. Hold hands and slide slowly across the smooth floor.
flow.say: Hold my hand. Push off and slide in your socks. Your feet keep touching the floor. That is sliding.
flow.kid: Hold a hand. Slide in your socks. Your feet stay on the floor.

ask.q: How is sliding different from rolling?
good: My feet stayed on the floor.
The same part touched the floor all the time.

flow.do: 1. Your child spins round slowly 3 times, arms out. 2. Then stands still and swings both arms back and forth.
flow.say: Spin round three times with your arms out. Then stop. Now swing your arms back and forth, like a swing.
flow.kid: Spin round three times. Stop. Now swing your arms back and forth.
flow.parent: Spinning is turning round in one place. Swinging is going back and forth from one point. Your arms swing from your shoulders.

flow.do: 1. Your child bounces on the spot on their toes 5 times. 2. Ask which of the five ways they liked best.
flow.say: Now bounce on your toes, five times. Feel your knees bend and spring. Which of the five ways did you like best?
flow.kid: Bounce on your toes five times. Which way did you like best?

check.q: You turned round and round in one place. Which way of moving was that?
check.why: Spinning is turning round in one place. Sliding is moving along while rubbing, and bouncing is springing back up.

activities.title: The Kitchen Motion Hunt
activities.context: In this activity you hunt in the kitchen for things that roll, slide, spin, swing or bounce, and sort them into five groups.

materials.item: 5 paper slips with ROLL, SLIDE, SPIN, SWING and BOUNCE, or a drawing for each
safe kitchen things: a lemon, an onion, a rolling pin, a steel plate, a steel tumbler, a ladle, a tea strainer, a ball

activities.safety: Use only safe, unbreakable things. Keep away from the stove, knives and the mixie.

schedule.what: Find kitchen things that move in each of the five ways and sort them onto the five slips.

activities.record: Draw one kitchen thing on each of the five slips.

setup.art: Five paper slips on a kitchen floor saying ROLL, SLIDE, SPIN, SWING and BOUNCE, with a small drawing on each.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the five slips.

setup.art: A girl rolling a lemon on the kitchen floor while she twirls a steel plate and a ladle swings on a hook.
setup.caption: 2. Try each thing. Put it on a slip.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the five slips. 2. Read each word with your child.
flow.say: Here are five slips: roll, slide, spin, swing and bounce. Let us find kitchen things for each one.
flow.kid: Here are five slips. Find a kitchen thing for each one.
flow.parent: A lemon or onion rolls. A steel plate slides on the floor and spins when twisted. A ladle swings on a hook. A ball bounces.

flow.do: 1. Your child tries each thing. 2. They put it on the slip for how it moved.
flow.say: Try the lemon. How did it move? Put it on that slip. Now try the plate.
flow.kid: Try each thing. How did it move? Put it on that slip.

ask.q: Can one thing go on two slips?
good: Yes, the plate slid and spun.
The ball rolled and bounced.

flow.parent: Let your child find that some things fit more than one slip. That is the main idea.

flow.do: 1. Look at the five groups together. 2. Ask which group has the most things.
flow.say: Which slip has the most things? Did anything move in two ways?
flow.kid: Which slip has the most? Did anything move two ways?

check.q: A ladle hangs on a hook. You tap it. Which way does it move?
check.why: A ladle hanging from a hook goes back and forth below the hook. That is swinging.

activities.title: Swing It: the bag on the door handle
activities.context: In this activity you hang a cloth bag on a door handle and give it one push. You watch how it swings back and forth, and count the swings until it stops.

materials.item: a cloth bag with handles, such as a jhola
an orange, a potato or a small steel tumbler to put inside
a door handle or a hook

schedule.what: Hang the bag, give it one push, count the swings, and find the still point it swings from.

activities.record: Draw the bag and the door handle. Draw a curved arrow going both ways under the handle.

setup.art: A cloth jhola with an orange inside hanging from a door handle.
setup.caption: 1. Put an orange in the bag. Hang it on the handle.

setup.art: A girl giving the hanging bag a small push, with a curved arrow showing it going back and forth.
setup.caption: 2. Give it one push. Count the swings.

flow.do: 1. Put the orange in the bag. 2. Hang the bag on the door handle so it hangs freely.
flow.say: Let us hang the bag on the handle. Which part do you think will move when we push it? Which part will stay still?
flow.kid: Hang the bag. Which part will move? Which part will stay still?

flow.do: 1. Your child gives the bag one gentle push. 2. Count each time it comes back to them, until it stops.
flow.say: Give it one gentle push. Now count each time it comes back to you. Keep counting until it stops.
flow.kid: Push the bag once. Count each time it comes back. Stop counting when the bag stops.

ask.q: Did it keep going for ever?
good: No, the swings got smaller and it stopped.
It slowed down.

flow.parent: It usually swings 10 to 20 times before it nearly stops. The air and the rubbing at the handle slow it down.

flow.do: 1. Point to the handle. 2. Ask your child to show the still point and the moving part.
flow.say: Show me the part that stayed still. Show me the part that swung. When you walk, which part of you swings from your shoulder?
flow.kid: Point to the still part. Point to the part that swung. What swings from your shoulder when you walk?

check.q: What stayed still while the bag swung?
check.why: A swinging thing hangs from one point that stays still. The bag hung from the handle and moved back and forth below it.

activities.title: Spin It: what spins, and where is its middle?
activities.context: In this activity you try to spin a steel plate, a bottle cap, a pencil and a book on the floor. You look for the middle point each one turns round.

materials.item: a steel plate
a bottle cap
a pencil
a thin book
a spinning top, such as a bambaram, if you have one

schedule.what: Spin four things on the floor and put a finger on the middle each one turns round.

activities.record: Draw each thing with a dot at the middle and a curved arrow round it.

setup.art: A steel plate, a bottle cap, a pencil and a thin book lying on a tiled floor.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the things to spin.

setup.art: A child's hand twisting a pencil lying on the floor so it spins round its middle, with a dot at the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Twist each one. Find the middle that stays put.

flow.do: 1. Show your child how to twist the plate flat on the floor so it spins.
flow.say: Twist the plate with your fingers and let go. Watch it spin round and round in one place.
flow.kid: Twist the plate. Let go. Watch it spin.
flow.parent: A steel plate spins well on a smooth tiled floor.

flow.do: 1. Your child spins the cap, the pencil and the book too. 2. For each, they point to the middle that does not move.
flow.say: Now spin the pencil. Which part of the pencil stays in one place? Point to it.
flow.kid: Spin the pencil. Which part stays in one place? Point to it.

ask.q: Where is the still middle of the pencil?
good: In the middle of the pencil.
The ends go round, the middle stays.

flow.do: 1. Ask which thing spun the longest. 2. Ask what made it stop.
flow.say: Which one spun the longest? Why did they all stop in the end?
flow.kid: Which spun the longest? Why did they stop?

check.q: A pencil spins on the floor. Which part moves round in the biggest circle?
check.why: A spinning thing turns round its middle. The middle stays put, and the ends travel round in the biggest circle.

flow.parent: Rubbing on the floor slows each one down. A plate or a top on its point often spins longest.

games.title: Five Ways: the sorting card game
games.players: A child and a grown-up who reads the cards. More children can join and take turns.
games.context: This is a card game. Each card names something that moves. The player puts it on the right mat: roll, slide, spin, swing or bounce.

items.f: A ball going down a slope
A chappal on a wet bathroom floor
An oonjal, a swing seat hanging in the hall
A rubber ball dropped on the floor
A coconut falling off a cart and going down the road
A child going down a slide in the park
A box pushed across the floor

printables.title: 5 mats (cut out, or write the words on five sheets of paper)

rules: Cut out the five mats, or write ROLL, SLIDE, SPIN, SWING and BOUNCE on five sheets of paper. Lay them on the floor.
Mix the 12 cards and make a pile, front side up. The grown-up reads the top card out loud.
The player shows that motion with their hands, then puts the card on a mat.
The grown-up turns the card over and reads the back. If the mat is right, the player keeps the card. The auto wheels card fits two mats, ROLL and SPIN, and either one is right.
If the player gives a good reason for a different mat, the player keeps the card too.
If the mat is wrong, the grown-up shows the right mat and slides the card under the pile for one more try. After a second wrong try, the card goes on its right mat and nobody keeps it.
The game ends when the pile is finished. The player with the most cards wins. When one child plays, try to keep 8 or more of the 12.

setup.art: Five sheets of paper on the floor labelled ROLL, SLIDE, SPIN, SWING and BOUNCE.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the five mats.

setup.art: A mother reading a card while a girl twirls her finger to show spinning before placing the card on the SPIN mat.
setup.caption: 2. Listen, show it with your hands, then put the card down.

flow.do: 1. Make the five mats. 2. Read each word together and act it out with hands.
flow.say: Here are five mats. Show me rolling with your hands. Now sliding, spinning, swinging and bouncing.
flow.kid: Show each one with your hands. Roll, slide, spin, swing, bounce.

flow.do: 1. Read the cards one by one. 2. Your child acts out the motion and puts the card on a mat. 3. Turn the card over and read the back.
flow.say: A ceiling fan. Show me with your hands how it moves. Which mat does it go on?
flow.kid: Listen. Show it with your hands. Put it on a mat.

ask.q: Why did you put the auto wheels on ROLL?
good: They go round and round along the road.
They turn as the auto moves.

flow.parent: Some cards fit two mats. Wheels roll along the road, and each wheel spins round its middle. Praise a good reason.

flow.do: Count the cards on each mat.
flow.say: Which mat has the most cards? Did any card fit two mats?
flow.kid: Count the cards on each mat.

check.q: A chappal moves on a wet floor, and the same part keeps touching the floor. Which mat?
check.why: When the same part keeps touching and rubbing along the floor, it is sliding.

games.title: Find It Fast: the motion slip game
games.players: A child and a grown-up who counts. More children can join and take turns.
games.context: This is a quick hunting game. You pick a slip, and you have until the count of 10 to find something in the room that moves that way and show it.
rules: Fold the five slips and put them in a steel tumbler.
The player picks one slip. The grown-up reads it.
Before 10, the player finds something in the room that moves that way and makes it move.
Each thing found wins a tick on the score sheet. Put the slip back and pick again.
Each player gets 5 turns. The player with the most ticks wins. If you play alone, try to beat your own total next time.

setup.art: Five folded paper slips in a steel tumbler, and a hand pulling one out.
setup.caption: 1. Pick a slip from the tumbler.

setup.art: A boy swinging a hanging towel on a hook while a grown-up counts on their fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Find something that moves that way before 10.

flow.do: 1. Fold the slips and put them in a tumbler. 2. Clear away breakable things.
flow.say: Pick a slip. I will read it. Then find something that moves that way, before I count to ten.
flow.kid: Pick a slip. Find something that moves that way. Be quick!

flow.do: 1. Your child picks slips and hunts. 2. Count slowly to 10 each time. 3. Tick the score sheet. 4. Stop after 5 turns each.
flow.say: Swing! One, two, three... What did you find? Show me how it swings.
flow.kid: Find it. Show how it moves. Get a tick!

ask.q: What did you find for SPIN?
good: The ceiling fan.
A bottle cap I twisted.
Me!

flow.parent: Your child's own body always counts. That helps when there is nothing left in the room to find.

flow.do: Count the ticks.
flow.say: Which one was hardest to find? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which was hardest to find? Why?

options: A rubber ball dropped on the floor
check.why: A rubber ball squashes when it hits the floor and springs back up. A towel on a hook swings, and a fan spins.

projects.title: A Swing for a Toy
projects.context: In this project you make a small swing for a soft toy, from a box, string and a broom handle across two chairs. Then you push it and watch it swing.

materials.item: a small cardboard box, such as a sweet box or a shoebox lid, for the seat
string or thick thread, about 4 arm-lengths
a broom handle or a long stick
2 chairs of the same height
a small soft toy
a pencil to make holes, and tape

projects.safety: A grown-up makes the holes in the box, because a pencil point can slip.

schedule.what: Make the seat, tie the strings, hang it from the stick across two chairs, and swing the toy.

projects.record: Draw your toy on the swing, with a curved arrow going both ways.

setup.art: Two chairs back to back with a broom handle resting across their backs.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a broom handle across two chairs.

setup.art: A small box with a string tied through each corner, the strings tied to the broom handle so the box hangs.
setup.caption: 2. Tie strings from the box to the stick.

setup.art: A soft toy sitting in the small box swing, swinging back and forth, and a girl giving a gentle push.
setup.caption: 3. Sit the toy in the box. Give a gentle push.

flow.do: 1. Put two chairs a little apart with their backs facing. 2. Lay the broom handle across the two backs, and tape it down so it cannot roll off.
flow.say: This stick is the top of our swing. The swing will hang from it.
flow.kid: Lay the stick across the chairs. The swing hangs from here.

flow.do: 1. Make a hole in each corner of the box with a pencil. 2. Tie a string through each hole. 3. Tie the strings to the stick so the box hangs level.
flow.say: Tie a string to each corner. Then tie them to the stick. Make the box hang flat, so the toy does not fall.
flow.kid: Tie the strings. Make the box hang flat.
flow.parent: Two strings at the front and two at the back work best. Tape can hold them if knots are hard.

flow.do: 1. Sit the toy in the box. 2. Your child gives one gentle push. 3. Watch it swing back and forth.
flow.say: Sit the toy in the swing. Give one gentle push. Where is the still point the swing hangs from?
flow.kid: Sit the toy in. Push gently. Watch the toy swing!

ask.q: Why does the swing come back to you?
good: It hangs from the stick, so it goes back and forth.
It goes up, then comes back down.

flow.do: Ask how to make it swing again after it stops.
flow.say: The swing has stopped. How can you make it swing again?
flow.kid: It stopped. How can you make it swing again?

check.q: The toy's swing slows down and stops. How do you make it swing again?
options: Wait, and it will start by itself
check.why: A swing slows down and stops unless it gets another push.

challenges.title: Make the Bottle Slide, Not Roll
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A plastic bottle lying on its side rolls away when you push it. Can you make it slide instead, while it still lies on its side?
challenges.problem: A water bottle lying on its side keeps rolling off the table. Can you make it slide when you push it, instead of rolling?
constraints: The bottle must lie on its side.
When you push it gently, it must slide and not roll.
materials: an empty plastic bottle with its cap on
a ball of atta dough or play clay
a piece of flat cardboard or a thin book
general: Wheels let things roll. A cycle skids when its wheels stop turning and slide along the road.
Many pencils have six flat sides, so they roll off the desk less easily than round ones.
A wedge pushed under a car wheel stops it rolling.
creative: Tape a piece of flat cardboard along the bottle, so the bottle lies on it and cannot turn.
Press a lump of dough on one side of the bottle. The lump works like a foot and stops the bottle turning.
Put the bottle inside a small box, so the flat box slides instead.
Tape the bottle onto a thin book, so the book slides.
challenges.your_turn: Try two ways to make the bottle slide. Which worked better? Why do you think so?

setup.art: A plastic bottle lying on its side on a table, rolling away from a hand that pushed it.
setup.caption: 1. Push the bottle. It rolls.

setup.art: The same bottle taped onto a flat piece of cardboard, sliding across the table when pushed.
setup.caption: 2. Change it so it slides when you push.

flow.do: 1. Lay the bottle on its side. 2. Your child pushes it gently and watches it roll.
flow.say: Push the bottle gently. What does it do? Now we want it to slide instead. How could we stop it rolling?
flow.kid: Push the bottle. It rolls. How can you make it slide?

good: It is round.
Its round side touches the table.

flow.do: 1. Your child tries one idea, then pushes. 2. Then tries a second idea.
flow.say: Try your idea. Push it gently. Did it roll or slide? Now try another idea.
flow.kid: Try your idea. Push it. Did it slide? Try another.
flow.parent: If your child is stuck, ask: what could stop it turning over? Any flat side or foot works.

flow.do: Ask which idea worked best and why.
flow.say: Which idea worked best? Why did it stop the bottle rolling?
flow.kid: Which idea worked best? Why?

check.q: You tape a bottle onto a flat piece of cardboard and push the cardboard. Why does the bottle slide and not roll?
options: The flat cardboard sits on the table, so the bottle cannot turn over
The tape makes the bottle round
check.why: The flat cardboard lies flat on the table, so the bottle cannot turn over. It slides instead.

items.p: Draw a line from each thing to how it moves.
pairs: A ball going down a slope
A rubber ball dropped on the floor
A plate pushed on a table
items.why: A fan turns round in one place, a swing goes back and forth, a ball on a slope turns over as it goes, a dropped rubber ball springs back up, and a pushed plate rubs along the table.

items.p: Draw the Roll or Slide Test: the dabba on its side and the dabba standing flat. Draw a long line for the one that went further.
items.a: The dabba on its side with a long line, and the dabba standing flat with a short line.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the rolling dabba went much further than the sliding one.
items.art: A blank box with a line for the floor.

items.p: Circle in blue the things that roll. Circle in red the things that slide.
items: A lemon pushed along the floor
A book pushed across a table
A child on a park slide
items.why: Rolling things turn over as they move along. Sliding things keep the same part touching and rubbing.

items.p: A ball of atta dough bounces as high as a rubber ball.
items.why: False. The dough squashes and stays squashed, so it does not bounce. The rubber ball springs back to round and bounces up.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why did the dabba go further when it rolled?
items.a: Because when it rolled it hardly rubbed the floor. Standing flat, its bottom rubbed and stopped it.
items.why: A strong answer says what the dabba did and talks about rubbing on the floor.

items.p: Three of these spin. Which one does not?
opts: A bag on a door handle
items.why: A bag on a door handle swings back and forth. The others turn round in one place, which is spinning.

items.p: Look at the girl moving her body five ways. Under each picture, say ROLL, SLIDE, SPIN, SWING or BOUNCE, and a grown-up writes it.
labels: Lying on a mat, turning over and over
In socks, gliding on the floor
Springing up and down on her toes
items.why: Each picture shows one of the five ways the body moved in Five Ways With My Body.
items.art: Five small drawings of a girl: rolling on a mat, sliding in socks, spinning, swinging her arms, bouncing on her toes.

items.p: Draw one thing in your kitchen that rolls, and one that swings.
items.a: For example, a lemon or rolling pin that rolls, and a ladle on a hook that swings.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a real kitchen thing for each, and an arrow showing how it moves.

items.p: In the Roll or Slide Test, the dabba slid 1 tile, then 2 tiles. How many tiles in all?
items.why: 1 and 2 make 3.

items.p: A thing that hangs from one point and goes back and forth is ___.
items.why: Swinging is going back and forth while hanging from one point, like the bag on the door handle.

worksheets.title: Why Things Move the Way They Do (stretch)

items.p: Anjali and her brother Rohan look at a round steel plate.

views.says: A plate can only slide. That is how plates move.
A plate can slide, spin or roll. It depends how you push it.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Try it with a plate, then say why. Then say one thing the other person might say back.
items.a: Anjali. A plate slides when pushed flat, spins when twisted, and rolls when stood on its edge.
items.why: A strong answer uses a test with a real plate. It also says why Rohan thought so: we usually only see plates slide on a table.

items.p: Draw the bag swinging on the door handle. Put a dot on the part that stays still.
items.a: A bag hanging below a handle, with a dot on the handle and a curved arrow under it.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the dot at the handle, the point the bag hangs and swings from.
items.art: A blank box with a door handle drawn at the top.

items.p: Many people think round things always roll. Say what you saw in the Roll or Slide Test that shows this is not always true.
items.a: The round dabba standing flat did not roll. It slid, because its flat bottom touched the floor.
items.why: A strong answer says the dabba standing flat was round, but it slid.

items.p: Put the Bounce Test in order.
items: Look at the shape after it lands
Hold it at the table edge and let go
a: Hold it at the table edge and let go
Look at the shape after it lands
items.why: First we guess, then we drop it, then we look at what happened to its shape.

items.p: A swing keeps going for ever after one push.
items.why: False. The bag on the handle swung smaller and smaller and stopped. A swing needs more pushes to keep going.

items.p: Why do suitcases have wheels?
items.why: A rolling wheel hardly rubs the floor, so a small pull moves a heavy suitcase. Without wheels it would scrape and slide.

items.p: A ceiling fan is spinning. Label the part that stays still and the part that moves round in the biggest circle.
a: Moves round in the biggest circle
items.why: A spinning thing turns round its middle. The tips are furthest from the middle, so they go round in the biggest circle.
items.art: A ceiling fan seen from below, with two arrows pointing at the middle and at a blade tip.

items.p: A thing that turns round and round in one place is ___.
items.why: Spinning is turning round in one place, like a fan or a top.

items.p: A worker has to move a heavy gas cylinder across the floor. Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: how could she move it most easily, and why is it easier?
items.a: She can tip it onto its round edge and roll it. Rolling rubs the floor much less than dragging.
items.why: A strong answer says to roll it and links this to the dabba rolling further than sliding.

items.p: A cart wheel rubs the road as much as a box dragged along the same road.
items.why: False. A wheel rolls, so only a little of it touches the road at a time. A dragged box rubs its whole bottom along the road.

items.p: Lakshmi, Kavya and their friend Arjun watch an auto go by.

views.says: The wheels roll along the road.
No, each wheel spins round its middle.
The whole auto slides along the road.

items.ask: Who is right? Can two of them be right at once? Say why.
items.a: Lakshmi and Kavya are both right. Each wheel spins round its middle while it rolls along the road. The auto does not slide, unless it skids.
items.why: A strong answer sees that one wheel can roll and spin at the same time, and that rolling is not sliding.

items.p: A pencil keeps rolling off the desk. What could you do to stop it rolling? Say why it would work.
items.a: Use a pencil with flat sides, or press a lump of dough on one side so it sits flat. A flat side or a lump stops it turning over.
items.why: A strong answer changes how the pencil touches the desk, as in Make the Bottle Slide, Not Roll.

items.p: A sock ball and a rubber ball are dropped from the same table. Only the rubber ball bounces well. What is the best reason?
opts: The socks squash but spring back only a little
The sock ball was dropped from lower down
items.why: Both fell from the same height. The socks squash but spring back only a little, so they push off the floor only weakly.

items.p: Draw a new toy that can roll, spin and bounce. Show with arrows how it does each one.
items.a: Any toy, such as a ball, with an arrow for rolling, a curved arrow for spinning, and an up arrow for bouncing.
items.why: A strong drawing shows one thing moving in three ways, with a clear arrow for each.

items.p: Sort these into: moves along the floor, or stays in one place.
items.why: Rolling and sliding things go from one place to another. A spinning top, a fan and a swinging bag move a lot, but stay in about the same place.

items.p: The Earth spins round once every day.
items.why: True. That is why the Sun seems to rise in the morning and set in the evening.

items.p: You ran the Roll or Slide Test. Your friend says: 'It went further rolling just because you pushed harder.' How could you show it was a fair test?
items.a: I slid the book from the start line to the stop line every time, so every push was the same.
items.why: A strong answer explains how the push was kept the same, and suggests trying again with the friend pushing.

items.p: Draw a line from each thing to why it moves that way.
pairs: It springs back to its shape
A dabba on its side goes far
A dabba standing flat stops soon
Its flat bottom rubs on the floor
items.why: Each way of moving has a reason: springing back for bouncing, and how much a thing rubs the floor for rolling and sliding.

items.p: A coconut rolls down a slope and hits a pile of sand. It stops. Why?
opts: The sand rubs against it and holds it
Coconuts can only roll a little way
items.why: Soft sand rubs and pushes against the coconut much more than a hard road, so it stops quickly.

items.p: Look at a cycle going along, and a cycle turned upside down on its seat. Label each: ROLL, SPIN or SWING.
labels: The wheels of a cycle going along the road
The back wheel of an upside-down cycle, turned by hand
A cloth bag hanging from the handlebar, moving back and forth
items.why: Wheels roll along the road. A wheel turned in the air spins round its middle. A hanging bag swings back and forth from the handlebar.
items.art: A woman riding a bicycle past a boy who turns the pedal of an upside-down bicycle, with a cloth bag hanging from a handlebar, and arrows pointing to the wheels, the upside-down wheel and the bag.

quiz.p: A ceiling fan turns round and round in one place. How does it move?
quiz.why: Spinning is turning round in one place.

quiz.p: You lie on a mat and turn over and over. What are you doing?
quiz.why: Rolling is turning over and over while moving along.

opts: A bag hanging on a door handle
A box pushed on the floor
quiz.why: A swinging thing hangs from one point and goes back and forth.

quiz.p: You must move a heavy round tin across the floor with a small push. What should you do?
opts: Lay it on its side and roll it
quiz.why: Rolling hardly rubs the floor, so a small push moves it. Sliding it standing up rubs its whole bottom.

quiz.p: A ball of atta dough falls on the floor. What happens?
opts: It goes flat and does not bounce
quiz.why: Dough squashes and stays squashed. It does not spring back, so it does not bounce.

quiz.p: You push a steel plate flat across the floor. How does it move?
quiz.why: The same flat part keeps touching and rubbing along the floor, so it slides.

quiz.p: A child finds a heavy box very hard to drag. What could help?
opts: Put it on a cart with wheels
Drag it more slowly on its side
quiz.why: A wheel rolls and hardly rubs the ground, so heavy things move with a small push.

quiz.p: You guess the dabba will go further standing flat. What should you do next?
opts: Test it, and see what happens
quiz.why: A guess is checked by a test. Push the dabba both ways with the same push and count the tiles.

quiz.p: A rolling pin goes over and over as it moves along the kitchen floor. How does it move?
quiz.why: Rolling is turning over and over while moving along.

quiz.p: What does a rubber ball do for a moment when it hits the floor?
opts: It squashes a little, then springs back
quiz.why: The ball squashes a little where it hits, then springs back to round and pushes itself up.

applications: Wheels on carts, cycles, autos, trains and suitcases make heavy things roll instead of slide.
Ball bearings are little steel balls inside fans, cycle wheels and skates. They let parts roll instead of rub.
Playground slides are smooth so that children slide down easily.
Balls for cricket, football and tennis are made to bounce well.
Potters spin clay on a wheel to shape round pots.
Swings, cradles and the oonjal in many Indian homes swing back and forth from a hook.

spotted.art: A woman potter sitting at a spinning wheel with wet clay rising into a pot.

spotted.text: A wooden oonjal swinging in a home in Kerala, Tamil Nadu or Gujarat.
spotted.art: A wooden swing seat hanging on chains from the ceiling of a home, two children sitting on it.

open_questions.q: Why does a rolling thing stop in the end?
open_questions.why_open: We know rolling hardly rubs. But a rolling ball still slows down and stops. Scientists know some reasons: the ball and the floor squash a tiny bit, and air pushes against it. Working out exactly how much each reason matters, for every kind of ball and floor, is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Who made the very first wheel, and where?
open_questions.why_open: The oldest wheels found are more than 5,000 years old, from several parts of the world. Nobody knows whether one group of people invented the wheel and others copied it, or whether people in different places found it on their own.

ask_kids: How do the wheels of a bus or an auto move?
Can you roll a rolling pin across the table? Does the rolling pin roll or slide?
Which parts of you swing when you walk?
Is the Earth rolling, spinning or swinging?
What in this room would bounce if you dropped it?

jokes.j: Why did the ball keep rolling?
What did the fan say to the top?
Why was the dough ball sad at the bounce test?
What is a swing's favourite music?
Why did the plate go to the playground?
What did the rubber ball say to the floor?
What did the dabba say after rolling across the room?
Why did the top get dizzy?
jokes.a: It spent all day going round in circles!

maths.problem: In the Roll or Slide Test, a rolling dabba went 9 tiles. The sliding dabba went 2 tiles. Which went further, and how many more tiles?
maths.answer: The rolling dabba went further, by 7 tiles.
maths.explain: Count on from 2 to 9: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. That is 7 more. So rolling went 7 tiles further with the same push.
maths.context: This is about the Roll or Slide Test, where you pushed the same dabba lying on its side and standing flat.
maths.why_maths: Taking the small number from the big one shows how much further rolling went.

maths.problem: In a Kitchen Motion Hunt, 4 things were put on ROLL, 2 on SLIDE, 3 on SPIN, 1 on SWING and 1 on BOUNCE. Which slip had the most things? Which slips had the fewest?
maths.answer: ROLL had the most, 4 things. SWING and BOUNCE had the fewest, with 1 each. Those were the hardest to find.
maths.explain: 4 is the biggest number, so ROLL had the most. 1 is the smallest, and two slips had 1. Many kitchen things are round, which may be why so many rolled.
maths.context: This is about the Kitchen Motion Hunt, where you sorted kitchen things onto five slips.
maths.why_maths: Counting each group shows which kind of motion is most common in a kitchen, and makes us ask why.

maths.problem: Two children each gave a cloth bag on a door handle one push and counted the swings. One counted 12 swings. The other counted 17. Put the counts in order, from fewest swings to most.
maths.explain: 12 is less than 17. So the order is 12 first, then 17.
maths.context: This is about Swing It, where you pushed a bag on a door handle once and counted the swings.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two counts shows which bag swung more times.

warmup.q: Name the five ways things move.
warmup.a: Roll, slide, spin, swing and bounce.

warmup.q: Does a ceiling fan roll or spin?
With the same push, does a dabba go further rolling or sliding?
warmup.a: Rolling. It hardly rubs the floor.

warmup.q: Why does a ball of dough not bounce?
What stays still when a bag swings on a door handle?
What does the Earth do once every day?

roots.context: We have rolled, slid, spun, swung and bounced, at home and with our own bodies. Now we ask what the Roll or Slide Test tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Roll or Slide Test, the same push made the dabba roll far on its side and slide only a little standing flat. It was the same dabba both times. Rolling rubs the floor much less than sliding. So how a thing touches the floor changes how far it goes.
deep_truth.habit: We often think how far a thing goes depends only on what it is and how hard we push. The Roll or Slide Test kept both the same and changed only how the dabba touched the floor.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Roll or Slide Test, the same dabba with the same push went many tiles rolling on its side and only one or two tiles sliding flat.

three.who_am_i: Your body can roll, slide, spin, swing and bounce. You are the same person, moving in many ways.
three.what_is_life: Humans and other animals move in these ways too. A snake slides along the ground, a monkey swings from branch to branch, and a child rolls, spins and bounces.
three.what_is_this_world: Everything in the world is moving somehow. Even the floor under you is spinning with the whole Earth.

roots.thread: Rolling, sliding, spinning, swinging and bouncing are five ways of moving, and one dabba or plate can do several of them. How a thing moves depends on how it is pushed and how it touches the floor. Everything is moving all the time, even the floor under you.

teachings.teaching: Thirty spokes meet at the hub, the middle of a wheel. It is the empty space at the centre that makes the wheel useful.
teachings.link: A wheel turns round its hub, and the hub stays in place. In Spin It, every spinning thing turned round a middle that stayed put.

teachings.teaching: The Greek thinker Heraclitus taught that everything moves and nothing stays still. You cannot step into the same river twice.
teachings.link: We found motion everywhere: in the kitchen, in our bodies, and even in a dabba that seems still, because the Earth under it is spinning.

science.text: Rolling rubs much less than sliding. That is why wheels need only a small push to move heavy loads.
The Earth spins round once a day. In India, the ground under you is carried round faster than an aeroplane flies.

other_view.view: Some people say a rolling dabba is fully explained by the forces on it and the way it touches the floor. For them, nothing more is going on in the dabba, and feeling belongs only to living beings with nerves.

practice.title: Still on a spinning Earth
practice.say: Sit on the floor and close your eyes. Sit very, very still. The floor is spinning with the whole Earth, and you are moving faster than an aeroplane. Can you feel it? Now roll gently onto your side and sit up. You felt that, because you changed how you were moving. A smooth, steady spin is very hard to feel.
practice.kid: Sit still. Shut your eyes. The Earth is spinning you round. Can you feel it? Now roll onto your side and sit up. Could you feel that?

ask: In the Roll or Slide Test, the dabba and the push were the same both times. So why did the dabba go further on its side?
When you sit very still, are you really still?
Is there anything in the world that is not moving at all?
roots.art: A girl sitting cross-legged with her eyes closed on a tiled floor, a steel dabba beside her, and through the window the curve of the turning Earth drawn faintly in the night sky.

how_we_found_out.context: Who made the first wheel, and was it for rolling? This card tells what people who study the past have found.
how_we_found_out.who: Potters in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq; early cart-makers in Mesopotamia and Europe; and the people of the Indus Valley cities, such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The wheel was first made for carts, to roll along the ground.
how_we_found_out.story: Many people think the first wheel was made for carts. But archaeologists, people who dig up and study the past, found something different. Many of them now think the first wheels did not roll at all. They spun. In Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, potters put clay on a flat round wheel and turned it, about 5,500 years ago. The clay spun round and round in one place while the potter shaped a round pot. Later, people stood wheels on their edge and fixed them to carts. Now the wheels rolled along the ground. A heavy load that was hard to drag could be pulled easily. The oldest wooden wheel found so far, from a marsh in Slovenia, is about 5,150 years old. In the Indus Valley cities of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, about 4,500 years ago, people made small clay toy carts with wheels that turn, and children may have played with them. The same round shape could spin flat or roll on its edge. Potters in India still spin clay on wheels today.

founder: ideas/by_topic/forces-and-movement.md: 'compare rolling vs sliding friction using toy cars' became the Roll or Slide Test with a steel dabba, 'use a rolling pin' joined the Kitchen Motion Hunt, 'spin a coin' became Spin It, and 'mime of a bouncing ball' joined Five Ways With My Body.

The Level 1 unit on how toys move uses a slope test, a drop-height bounce test and a colour top. This unit uses a flat-floor push test with one dabba two ways, a bounce test of five materials from one height, a swinging bag and a toy swing instead.
science: Rolling resistance is far smaller than sliding friction for hard wheels on hard floors. Any introductory physics text.
Ball deformation during a bounce: slow-motion studies of tennis and rubber balls on hard surfaces.
Earth's rotation speed at the latitudes of India, about 1,400 to 1,650 kilometres an hour, against airliner cruising speeds of about 900 kilometres an hour.
Early potter's wheels in Mesopotamia from about the 4th millennium BCE, and the Ljubljana Marshes wheel, Slovenia, dated to about 3150 BCE.
Terracotta toy carts with wheels from Harappan sites, about 2600 to 1900 BCE.
Tao Te Ching chapter 11, and Plato, Cratylus 402a, on Heraclitus.

playtest: Walked through every game, experiment, activity, project and challenge as a parent and a 6 to 7 year old in a flat, with the listed things only. Both games now say what happens after a wrong answer and how they end, with a winner for two players or more. The toy swing now has enough string, the bottle challenge asks about the bottle instead of pencils, and the family-assuming people and made-up names were taken out of steps and art. Repeated questions about the dabba and the dough ball, one weak joke and two repeated quiz questions were removed, and the hedge on who made the first wheel was softened. In a second walk-through, the auto wheels card in the sorting game now says that ROLL and SPIN are both right, and the swing-count maths question now matches the bag-on-the-handle activity, where swings are counted, instead of a toy swing project that never counted.
